summary:
Tasmania's own statutory layer sits on top of the national framework. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics. A September 2013 amendment extended protection to transgender and intersex people and prohibited conduct that offends, humiliates, intimidates, insults or ridicules a person on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity. Later amendments added gender expression, gender identity (including being transgender or transsexual and identifying or living as another gender), and sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics as grounds, and brought those grounds within the incitement-of-hatred prohibition.

A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 that explicitly includes gender identity and sexual orientation within the 1997 sentencing act. The upper house had not voted at the time of the source.

The age of consent is 17 and is equal for all forms of sexual activity, a threshold Tasmania shares only with South Australia.

Conversion therapy practices remained legally permitted in Tasmania as of September 2026.

No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern is documented for Tasmania.

Same-sex couples can enter registered domestic partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony, and adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories from April 2018.
tangentialFactors:
Tasmania was the last Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexuality, with effect from 14 May 1997, after it refused to repeal its Criminal Code provisions following the commencement of the Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 on 19 December 1994 and faced a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania.

The penalties for the offences it retained were up to 21 years, described as the harshest in the Western world.

Tasmania was the only Australian state to have criminalised cross-dressing, an offence under the Police Offences Act 1935 until repealed in 2001.

Decriminalisation followed the United Nations Human Rights Committee decision in Toonen on 31 March 1994 and section 4 of the federal Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change is governed by 2019 amendments to the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1999, which received royal assent on 8 May 2019 and took effect on 5 September 2019. They require only a simple declaration, with no forced divorce, sex reassignment surgery or other medical requirement.

From 8 May 2019 Tasmania permits self-declared gender registration for Tasmanian-registered births with no medical certificate or medical document required. A person aged 16 or older may register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary or another self-described gender neither entirely male nor entirely female, by statutory declaration of identity and lived or sought gender, subject to a Registrar power to refuse non-prescribed terms. Parents or guardians may register a gender for under-16s, supported by the child's declaration where able or statements of consistency with the child's will and preference, with optional counselling evidence where the child is under 18. Birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and unchangeable except to correct an initial error, but ceases upon gender registration.

The same laws allow parents to choose whether a child's gender is recorded, allow individuals to remove a gender descriptor entirely, allow parents to change the legal gender of their children, and extend the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth.

Historic convictions are eligible for expungement under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017, effective 9 April 2018. Charges and convictions for cross-dressing offences under section 8(1)(d) of the Police Offences Act 1935 as in force before 12 April 2001, including attempts and inciting, instigating, aiding or abetting, are eligible on application to the Secretary by the charged person or, if deceased or lacking capacity, by specified representatives; the Act received royal assent on 21 November 2017. Convictions for homosexual sexual offences prior to 1997 are also eligible. Compensation payments of up to $75,000 take effect from 2 August 2026, following an official parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017.

As of 2019 Tasmania issues X sex descriptors on birth certificates.
outOfScopeNotes:
The hate crimes bill that passed the lower house in September 2025 had not been voted on by the upper house, so its inclusion of gender identity and sexual orientation in the 1997 sentencing act is not yet in force.

Conversion therapy remained legally permitted in Tasmania as of September 2026; no legislation prohibiting it is sourced.

The Tasmanian Government opposed the 2019 birth-certificate and gender-recognition amendments and declined to rule out later repeal.
